short: SUPERSEDED in April 2026 by SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13. What the revised interagency model risk guidance changes for AI.
title: SR 11-7 and the 2026 Model Risk Guidance
subtitle: Superseded April 2026 by SR 26-2 and OCC 2026-13
body_html:
On this page

  • What changed in April 2026
  • What SR 26-2 means for AI
  • How to align AI model risk management with SR 26-2: a 5-step path
  • Frequently asked questions
  • Historical: SR 11-7 as it stood from 2011 to April 2026
  • Primary sources

The one-paragraph answer

SR 11-7 has been superseded. On April 17, 2026 the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC issued revised interagency model risk management guidance: Federal Reserve SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management, and OCC Bulletin 2026-13. SR 26-2 supersedes and replaces SR 11-7 (April 4, 2011) and SR 21-8, the 2021 interagency statement on model risk for BSA/AML systems. The core discipline survives, model inventory, independent validation, governance and controls, but four things changed that matter for AI: the guidance states that it is not enforceable and that noncompliance will not by itself draw supervisory criticism; it is expected to be most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets; it narrows the definition of a model to complex quantitative methods; and it places generative and agentic AI outside its scope, pending a request for information on banks' use of AI.

This page keeps its old address because people still search for SR 11-7. Everything above the historical section describes the guidance in force now. The section marked historical describes SR 11-7 as it stood until April 2026 and is kept for reference.

What changed in April 2026

On April 17, 2026 the three agencies replaced the 2011 guidance. Federal Reserve SR 26-2 supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8. OCC Bulletin 2026-13 rescinds OCC Bulletin 2011-12 (the OCC counterpart to SR 11-7), OCC Bulletin 2021-19 (the BSA/AML model risk statement), OCC Bulletin 1997-24 (credit scoring models), and the Model Risk Management booklet of the Comptroller's Handbook. The agencies describe the revision as clarifying model risk management principles and setting out a risk-based approach tailored to each banking organisation's model risk profile and the size and complexity of its operations.

The guidance says it is not enforceable

The revised text states that it does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements, and that noncompliance with it will not result in supervisory criticism. SR 11-7 contained no equivalent statement. This does not mean model risk is unsupervised: the guidance notes that supervisory action may still result from violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices stemming from insufficient management of model risk. But it is now framed as principles rather than as an examination checklist.

A $30 billion relevance threshold

The guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets. It may also be relevant to smaller institutions with significant exposure to model risk because of the prevalence and complexity of their models or activities outside traditional community banking. The agencies are reining in the practice of applying large-bank model risk expectations to community institutions.

The definition of "model" narrowed

A model is now a complex quantitative method, system or approach that applies statistical, economic or financial theories to process input data into quantitative estimates. Simple arithmetic calculations, such as those in spreadsheets, and deterministic rule-based processes and software with no such theory underpinning them are expressly excluded. Under SR 11-7 essentially any quantitative method producing an estimate was a model. That reading no longer holds automatically.

A clearer risk taxonomy

The revised guidance says model risk is influenced by a model's inherent risk, exposure, purpose and use, and that purpose together with exposure determines a model's materiality. It also states that using a model beyond its intended purpose introduces additional uncertainty and risk, which is precisely the failure mode AI tools invite.

What SR 26-2 means for AI

A footnote to the revised guidance draws the line. Generative AI and agentic AI models are described as novel and rapidly evolving, and are not within the scope of the guidance. Its principles apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models. The same footnote says a banking organisation's own risk management and governance practices should still determine the governance and controls for any tools the guidance does not cover.

So a machine-learning credit model that meets the definition of a model is in scope, and a large language model assistant is not, but the second still needs governing. The agencies have said they plan to issue a request for information on model risk management generally and on banks' use of AI in particular, including generative AI, agentic AI and AI-based models. That is where the AI-specific questions will be asked, and banks with material AI deployments should plan to respond rather than watch.

How to align AI model risk management with SR 26-2: a 5-step path

This is the sequence that works. Start with what you actually run, not with the framework.

  1. Inventory the AI in scope. List every model and AI system that could fall under SR 26-2. Record what it does, what decision it influences, what data it touches, and who owns it. Mark which systems are generative or agentic AI, which the guidance leaves outside its scope, so they are governed under your own framework rather than dropped from view.
  2. Determine whether you are actually in scope. Work out which of your systems meet SR 26-2's narrower definition of a model, and whether your institution is above the $30 billion threshold or carries significant model risk below it. Write the determination down with its reasoning. A documented scope determination is defensible. An undocumented assumption is not.
  3. Assign one accountable owner. Name a person, not a committee, with the authority to stop a deployment. Governance without someone who can say no is documentation, not control.
  4. Build the evidence file. Assemble the documentation the guidance describes: model development and use, validation and monitoring, governance and controls, and the treatment of vendor models. The guidance is not enforceable in itself, but supervisory action can still follow from unsafe or unsound practices, and the file is what shows yours are not.
  5. Set a review cadence and hold it. Re-run the assessment on a schedule tiered by materiality, which SR 26-2 ties to a model's exposure and purpose, and after any material change to the model, the data, or the use case. A control tested once is a snapshot, not a control.

Frequently asked questions

Is SR 11-7 still in force?

No. SR 11-7 was superseded on April 17, 2026 by SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management, issued jointly by the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC. The OCC's counterpart, Bulletin 2011-12, was rescinded the same day by OCC Bulletin 2026-13. Current compliance documentation should cite SR 26-2; SR 11-7 is historical.

Does SR 26-2 cover generative AI?

No. The revised guidance says generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving and are not within its scope. Its principles apply to traditional statistical and quantitative models and to non-generative, non-agentic AI models, and it says a bank's own risk management and governance practices should still determine the controls for tools it does not cover.

Does the 2026 guidance apply to my community bank?

It is expected to be most relevant to institutions above $30 billion in total assets. Smaller institutions with significant model risk exposure may still find it relevant, but the agencies were explicit that they are correcting the over-application of large-bank model risk expectations to community banks. If your prior model risk programme was built by copying a large-bank framework, this is the moment to right-size it.

What counts as a "model" now?

Under the 2026 guidance, a complex quantitative method, system or approach that applies statistical, economic or financial theories to process input data into quantitative estimates. Simple arithmetic calculations and deterministic rule-based processes are expressly excluded. This is narrower than the 2011 definition, under which arguably every AI system and every decisioning spreadsheet qualified. A complex machine-learning model driving credit decisions is still a model. A deterministic rules engine with an AI label on the box is not.

What is the difference between this and the NIST AI RMF?

The banking guidance is sector-specific and focused on model risk. NIST AI RMF is horizontal, voluntary, and covers AI-specific risk categories the banking guidance does not address at all, including bias, explainability and AI-specific security. With SR 26-2 explicitly non-enforceable and generative AI outside its scope, the AI overlay matters more, not less: it is now where the AI-specific questions actually get answered.

How does SR 26-2 interact with ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001 alignment supports model risk management under SR 26-2 but does not substitute for it. ISO/IEC 42001 gives you the AI management system structure; SR 26-2 describes the model risk practices banking supervisors look for. Banks using AI should build both, and the management system is the natural home for the generative AI the banking guidance leaves out.

Where does SR 11-7 show up in SRJ's work?

Volume III of The Operating Discipline for AI Library™ includes an SR 11-7 crosswalk in Appendix L, mapping SRJ artifacts (Accountability Matrix, AI Vendor Risk Inventory™, dossiers, Board Reporting Package™) to SR 11-7 requirements. The crosswalk was written against SR 11-7, which SR 26-2 has since replaced. Banks pursuing the AI Business Enablement Audit™ get the model risk gap analysis included.

Historical: SR 11-7 as it stood from 2011 to April 2026

Historical text. Everything in this section describes SR 11-7, which was superseded on April 17, 2026 by SR 26-2. It is kept because SR 11-7 is still cited in contracts, audit findings and vendor documentation written before April 2026. Do not rely on it as current guidance.

What SR 11-7 was

SR 11-7 was Supervisory Letter 11-7, "Guidance on Model Risk Management," issued by the Federal Reserve Board on April 4, 2011. Its OCC counterpart was Bulletin 2011-12, "Sound Practices for Model Risk Management," issued the same day. (Earlier versions of this page cited OCC Bulletin 2013-29 as the counterpart. That was an error. 2013-29 is third-party relationships risk management guidance, a different document.) The FDIC adopted the same framework in 2017, which made it the universal US banking standard for model risk for fifteen years, and examiners cited it across the regulated banking system.

Regulators were consistent from 2011 about what a model was: a quantitative method that processes input data into output for decision-making. Nearly every AI system met that definition, so the model inventory, validation, monitoring and governance obligations SR 11-7 established for statistical models were read as applying to AI. Banks that had not expected this, after rolling out an AI tool for fraud detection, an LLM assistant for customer service, or a machine-learning model for compliance monitoring, found examiners asking for the model inventory entry, the validation and the owner.

What SR 11-7 required: three pillars

SR 11-7 was organised around three pillars: model development and use, model validation, and governance and controls.

Model development, implementation, and use. Every model had to be built for a specific purpose, developed with documented data, and implemented with controls that checked whether it was being used within its intended scope. Documentation had to be thorough enough that an independent reviewer could reproduce the model's construction. For AI, that meant training data documentation, feature engineering choices, hyperparameter selection rationale and model-selection reasoning.

Model validation. Independent validation was the heart of SR 11-7. Every model had to be validated by a party who did not develop it, before it was used in production, covering conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis. For AI, validation was read to include bias testing, robustness testing, adversarial evaluation and drift monitoring, by a validator with the authority, expertise and independence to challenge the developers.

Governance, policies, and controls. Model risk management had to be a written programme with board oversight, senior management accountability, defined roles, a model inventory, risk tiering, policies for approval and use, and change control. The model inventory was the artifact examiners asked for: every model in use, its purpose, risk tier, owner, validation status, last review date and performance history.

Third-party model risk under SR 11-7

A bank that used a model built by a vendor remained accountable for it. Buying an LLM, a fraud model from a fintech, or an AI decisioning platform did not shift model risk management responsibility to the vendor, and vendor contracts were expected to include information sharing, validation cooperation, incident notification and audit rights. SR 26-2 also addresses vendor and other third-party products, including their validation.

Why SR 11-7 mattered

For banks, SR 11-7 findings on AI model inventories led to Matters Requiring Attention, and repeat findings could escalate. For bank vendors, it flowed through contracts as requests for validation cooperation, model documentation and audit rights. For non-bank fintechs, insurers and credit-adjacent firms, it became the reference framework by analogy, with insurance and state financial regulators asking for SR 11-7-style model governance where the letter did not formally apply.

What the research said about SR 11-7

The academic literature on SR 11-7 was ahead of most corporate practice. Two findings remain worth putting in front of any executive who thinks model governance is a formality.

“ML can be less transparent and explainable than traditional regression models, which may raise unique questions about compliance”

Brotcke, Journal of Risk and Financial Management (2022)

“regulators demand these models to be transparent and auditable”

Bücker, Szepannek, Gosiewska & Biecek, Journal of the Operational Research Society (2020)

Primary sources

The authoritative texts behind this summary. Where a compliance decision turns on exact wording, read the source, not a secondary summary, including this one.
